title: Day nine
setting: Nine good days, then a weekend.

lines.t: Nine days of running, then I missed Thursday and Friday.
So you've fallen off the wagon.
Completely.
After two days? That's a weekend.
It always starts like this.
Then get back on track on Monday and stop counting from one.
The counting is what keeps me going.
Until it doesn't. Build a habit around something already fixed in your daily routine, like coffee.
Run before coffee, you mean.
And stick to it on the bad days by going for ten minutes instead of forty. Ten minutes still counts.

title: Midnight is not late
setting: Somebody who has described himself as a night owl for twenty years.

lines.t: I'm a night owl. I always have been.
What time do you actually stop working?
Midnight, usually. Then I can't sleep until two.
The screen at midnight is doing half of that.
I oversleep every Saturday to make up for it.
And you feel worse on Sunday.
Always.
Have a lie-in of two hours and you're fine. Five hours moves your whole week.
So what do I do?
Wind down for an hour. Something boring, something on paper. You can't unwind with a laptop open.
That's the sleep hygiene thing everybody talks about.
It's dull and it works. Get an early night twice this week and see whether you feel well rested by Friday.
And the downtime at weekends?
Protect it. You can't recharge in the gaps between things, and you've been trying to for a year.

title: The phone in the kitchen
setting: Two colleagues compare notes on screen time.

lines.t: My screen time said six hours forty a day. I checked it twice.
What did you delete?
Nothing. I moved my charger to the kitchen.
That's all?
The first three nights were strange. I reached for a phone that wasn't there.
And now?
Four hours, and the last hour of the day is completely different.
I tried that once. I use my phone as an alarm clock.
So buy an alarm clock. Mine cost seven euro.
That is annoyingly simple. All right, I'll try it this week.

title: Four hours and eleven minutes
setting: The weekly screen report arrives and it is worse than expected.

lines.t: My phone says four hours and eleven minutes yesterday.
Of screen time?
Outside work. That's the frightening part.
Where does it go?
News, mostly. At night, in bed.
That's doomscrolling, and it has a name because everybody does it.
Should I do a digital detox? A friend went a week without a phone.
A week is a holiday. Turn off every notification except calls, and that's most of the battle won.
Even messages?
Especially messages. Then unplug after ten at night and leave the phone in another room, so picking it up is a decision instead of a reflex.

title: Saying no in November
setting: A brother and sister talk about too many commitments.

lines.t: Two committees, a weekend course, and the neighbour's renovation.
Do you enjoy any of them?
I attend all of them. That's not the same thing.
Write down why you said yes to each one.
That feels uncomfortable.
Do it anyway. I'll wait.
Seven of eleven say the same thing. It felt rude to refuse.
So cancel three tonight and see what actually happens.
And if people are offended?
Then you'll know. My guess is nobody will be, and that will annoy you.

title: You said yes again
setting: A fourth weekend in a row given away to other people.

lines.t: You said yes to the Saturday thing.
I know.
That's the fourth weekend in a row.
I feel overwhelmed just reading my own calendar.
Then you have to learn to say no, and say it early.
It sounds rude when I say it.
'I can't this time' is a complete sentence. Nobody has ever needed the reason.
I don't even have the headspace to work out what I want.
Which is why you set boundaries in advance. One weekend a month is yours before anybody asks for it.
Me time sounds so self-indulgent.
Call it whatever you like. Self-care is a silly phrase for something people our age need in order to keep working.
So I make time for myself, slow down, and stop trying to manage stress by adding things to the list.

title: We cancel every time
setting: Two friends who arrange things and then don't do them.

lines.t: We make plans and then somebody cancels them.
Usually me.
Usually both of us.
It's easier to cancel plans than to explain that I'm tired.
Then let's make it smaller. Coffee on Saturday morning, one hour.
That I would keep.
And I want to catch up with Rada properly, in person.
Then see her without the children for once. An hour of quality time beats an afternoon of shouting.
I've also been thinking about picking up a hobby again.
The pottery?
Or I could volunteer at the shelter on Sundays. It's the one place I socialise where nobody is checking a phone.

title: Two hundred leva in a box
setting: Three weekends of clearing out, and what came of it.

lines.t: I sold four boxes of things I'd forgotten I owned.
How much?
Two hundred leva. And the flat feels twice the size.
So the declutter worked.
It started as a spring clean and it took three weekends.
What are you doing with the money?
Saving up for a proper desk. The kitchen table is destroying my back.
Does the translation work still bring anything in?
It's a side hustle rather than a salary. Three hundred a month, sometimes.
That's enough to live within your means without counting every coffee.

title: An hour each way
setting: Ten hours a week on a bus, and an offer to move.

lines.t: The commute is an hour each way now.
Ten hours a week.
I work from home on Tuesdays and Thursdays, which helps.
Does it? You start at seven on those days.
Because I can.
And you never switch off, because the laptop lives in the kitchen.
I take a break at lunch.
You eat at the desk. I've watched you do it.
They've offered me the Varna office.
Would you relocate?
Maybe. It takes a year to settle in anywhere, and I'd rather spend that year settling in than sitting on a bus.

title: Say it out loud
setting: Eleven resolutions in January and none of them left by March.

lines.t: I set goals every January and forget them by March.
How many?
Eleven, this year.
There's the problem. Eleven goals is a wish list.
So one?
One that changes something, and one that frightens you slightly.
The presentation in English at the conference.
That's exactly it. You'd step out of your comfort zone, badly, in front of people.
Which is what I'm afraid of.
Personal growth is mostly a series of things you did badly the first time. Say yes now, while it's still far away.
